power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) is a database comprising word reading data for 9,961 of the most frequently printed English words for children, including continuous IRTbased estimates of word reading difficulty, accompanying word characteristics, and raw triallevel data.
Data on isolated word reading accuracy were collected from 1,907 children in grades 1-5 across multiple US sites.

Each child read a list of words ranging from 250 to 500 items depending on reading skill (less proficient children were often unable to finish the entire list of words), with each list representing the full distribution of word difficulties oversampled for words at the child's reading level.
Each child also attempted 99 linking items representing the full distribution of word difficulties.
A total of 631,322 responses were collected with the average child providing 336.

More recent investigations have expanded the range of lexical variables examined, incorporating semantic characteristics (e.g., imageability, concreteness, and age of acquisition), morphological structure, orthographic and phonological neighborhood measures, and indices of spelling-sound consistency (e.g., Apfelbaum et al., 2013; Kearns et al., 2016; Steacy et al., 2019; Kellenberger et al., 2024; Yap et al., 2012).

text.text: Collectively, this work has shown that word-level characteristics account for meaningful variation in children's word reading performance and that the influence of these characteristics often interacts with child-level factors such as decoding skill, reading experience, and vocabulary knowledge.
Despite these advances, most developmental studies have been limited by relatively small word samples, often ranging from a few dozen to a few hundred words.
As a result, estimates of the influence of lexical characteristics may be constrained by the particular words selected for study.

Large-scale item-level databases such as the developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) provide an opportunity to examine lexical influences across thousands of words spanning a broad range of difficulty levels and lexical characteristics.

Such databases can support more comprehensive investigations of how established lexical characteristics-including frequency, length, transparency, semantic variables, and neighborhood structure-contribute to word reading difficulty in developing readers and provide a foundation for evaluating the contribution of emerging theoretically motivated predictors.

Attempts to explore, understand, and predict the combined effects of multiple word-level characteristics on word reading accuracy in developing readers have been constrained by several limitations in the developmental reading literature.

These include: (1) although the field has produced several large-scale databases of word recognition -commonly referred to as "lexicon projects" and related "crowdsourcing projects" (e.g., Adelman et al., 2014; Balota et al., 2007; Keuleers et al., 2012; Mandera et al., 2020) -these resources primarily reflect adult reading behavior; (2) empirical studies of word reading acquisition have predominantly focused on monosyllabic, monomorphemic words (e.g., Balota et al., 2007; Coltheart et al., 2001; Perry et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2011; Seidenberg & McClelland, 1989; Siegelman et al., 2020; Yap & Balota, 2009); (3) most developmental studies rely on small samples of both children and words and employ factorial designs with limited control variables (e.g., Strain, Patterson, & Seidenberg, 2002); and (4) publicly available developmental databases generally do not provide worddifficulty estimates linked to the lexical, orthographic, and functional characteristics of words commonly encountered in children's print input, including both published (e.g., Korochkina & Rastle, 2025) and unpublished (e.g., Dawson et al., 2023) sources.

text.text: To address these limitations, we developed the developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP), a publicly available relational database containing continuous item response theory (IRT)-based estimates of oral word-reading difficulty for 9,961 high-frequency English words encountered by U.S. children in Grades 1-5, together with a broad set of accompanying word characteristics.
The database was designed to support detailed modeling of the lexical and orthographic properties that contribute to word-reading difficulty across a large number of items

text.text: The d-ELP extends this work in several important respects.

First, rather than reporting performance on a fixed set of items, the d-ELP uses an item response theory (Rasch) framework within a planned-missing design, with a common set of linking items used to place word-difficulty estimates on a shared developmental scale.
This approach permits direct comparison of difficulty estimates across nearly 10,000 words even though individual children completed only a subset of the full item pool.
Second, the d-ELP substantially expands the lexical coverage of developmental databases.
Third, whereas the DLP was developed for German, a relatively transparent orthography, the d-ELP focuses on English, whose quasi-regular orthography presents unique challenges for developing readers.

Finally, whereas the DLP examined lexical decision and naming performance, the d-ELP was designed to estimate oral word reading 1 difficulty, a construct that is directly aligned with developmental theories of English word reading acquisition and with educational assessment and instructional practice.

We acknowledge that some large-scale adult databases have incorporated both naming and lexical decision measures; however, our objective was to develop a resource that would be maximally informative for understanding and assessing children's developing word reading skill.
Consequently, the d-ELP difficulty estimates should be interpreted as indices of oral word reading difficulty rather than as a broader measure of lexical knowledge or lexical processing.

More broadly, the database provides developmental data for evaluating and refining computational models of word-reading development; constructing instructional materials appropriate for developing readers and spellers, including AI-based assessment and instructional systems; and developing more precise, developmentally appropriate formative and summative assessments of word-reading skill.

The project was also motivated by continuing questions about the magnitude of effects associated with specific word-level variables and about which variables should be incorporated as controls in factorial experiments and individual-differences studies (see Balota, Yap, Hutchison, & Cortese, 2012; Brysbaert, Keuleers, & Mandera, 2014; Keuleers & Balota, 2015).

text.text: In this introduction to the d-ELP we describe the motivation for this project; the methods used for data collection; the analytic framework used to establish a continuous measure of word reading difficulty across a wide swath of printed words; descriptive statistics of the relational database; and an overview of the functionality of the publicly available relational database that provides searchable access to the oral word difficulty ratings and associated word-level statistics for each of the stimuli (along with the raw trial-level data).

We also demonstrate the d-ELP's ability to estimate the impact of general word-level predictors (e.g., frequency, word length, transparency, semantic measures, and orthographic neighborhood size) on word recognition performance in developing readers to help demonstrate the potential of the database to inform mechanisms associated with early word reading development and identify potentially important word characteristics to be included in smaller scale experiments of word reading performance in developing readers.
It is important to note that the word difficulty estimates provided by the d-ELP reflect difficulty in oral word reading rather than a broader construct of lexical knowledge.

Although oral word reading is strongly influenced by orthographic, phonological, semantic, and morphological characteristics, successful performance on a word naming task does not necessarily imply complete knowledge of a word's meaning, nor does knowledge of a word's meaning guarantee accurate pronunciation.

Consequently, the d-ELP should be interpreted as providing item-level estimates of oral word reading difficulty, a construct that is highly relevant to developmental theories of reading acquisition as well as educational assessment and intervention.
For simplicity we use "word difficulty" throughout the manuscript to refer to "oral word reading difficulty in developing readers".

text.text: In the Steacy study, the probability of reading a nonword such as zeam vs. zead (with either the higher frequency pronunciation of ea as /i/ vs. the lower frequency pronunciation of ea as /ɛ/) was dependent on a child's word reading skill and the corpus-based rime support for the vowel pronunciation (-eam supports ea as /i/ whereas -ead supports ea as /ɛ/).

Results suggest that general reading skill at the child level and rime support at the nonword level uniquely facilitate context-dependent vowel pronunciations in our sample of developing readers (i.e., zeam read to rhyme with team and zead to rhyme with head).

Results were interpreted by Steacy et al. within a statistical learning framework (i.e., a child-by-word framework), supporting a developmental model of word reading in which children are more likely to use an alternative vowel pronunciation in a nonword as they become more proficient readers and as the occurrence of the alternative vowel pronunciation is increasingly supported by the corpus of words experienced.

As would be expected in such a model of word reading development, child and corpus attributes work to tune variant vowel pronunciations across individual children and words, with important variance associated with both factors.

These relatively simple examples -varied vowel pronunciations of the digraph ea in single-syllable words (e.g., -eat pronunciations) and nonwords across two fairly frequent rime patterns (-eam vs. -ead) -illustrates one of the most persistent challenges posed by quasiregular orthographies such as English: accurately predicting word reading difficulty in developing readers while accounting for word characteristics such as frequency, age of acquisition, phonological and morphological complexity, orthographic neighborhood size, and concreteness.

Predictive models are essential for quantifying how word-level features interact with child-level knowledge and skill across development -for example, capturing the shift from reliance on simple spelling-sound correspondences to greater use of morphological and syllabic structure during word reading development (see Castles, Rastle, & Nation, 2018) -while also enabling the testing and refinement of theoretical accounts of lexical development and word recognition.

text.text: Achieving this goal, however, is complicated by the quasi-regular nature of English, which poses significant challenges for generating accurate predictive models across a wide range of words.

Existing models tend to be underspecified and often biased by our limited ability to fully capture the quasiregular relations that determine word reading difficulty across words and children (e.g., Lim et al., 2024; Siegelman, Kearns, et al., 2020; Steacy et al., 2022).

text.text: As a result, the explanatory power of word difficulty predictive models is constrained, reducing their utility for advancing our theoretical understanding of word reading development and providing limited input to instructional design.

To illustrate the nature and potential severity of the problem of predicting difficulty across a broad range of word characteristics, we pooled child and word data across multiple studies with the intent of developing a word-level prediction model of accuracy that could be used for predicting items difficulty (Grade Equivalent) on the 63 words from the Woodcock-Johnson-III Letter-Word Identification (WJ3-LWID; Woodcock et al., 2001) task.

text.text: Accuracy data from 349 words pooled across five datasets, along with 16 word-level predictors (representing psycholinguistic word properties as well as measures of behavioral performance from the adult ELP), were used as training data to develop a general word difficulty predictive model which was subsequently applied to predict item difficulty on the WJ3-LWID items (for details on the sample and analytic approach see the supplemental materials).
Based on the pooled data an additive linear regression model predicting (known) accuracy scores was fit from all predictors with the adjusted-R² of this model being 71.7%.
This model was applied to the list of 63 WJ3-LWID items (pseudo-R² was estimated at 60.4%) and the relation between the predicted accuracy scores and WJ's GE scores plotted (Figure 2).

These results underscore the need for a large-scale behavioral database capturing word reading difficulties across a wide range of word characteristics while sampling the full age range of reading skills in English-speaking children in the early stages of learning to read.

text.text: Understanding the complex interplay between children's skills and knowledge and the characteristics of words across development remains a critical challenge from both theoretical and instructional perspectives.

To help address this need, we introduce the d-ELP -a companion to the English Lexicon Project (Balota et al., 2007) -as an initial resource for examining how English orthography shapes word reading development in children across a large corpus of words.
text.formatted: To help address this need, we introduce the d-ELP -a companion to the English Lexicon Project <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Balota et al., 2007)</ref> -as an initial resource for examining how English orthography shapes word reading development in children across a large corpus of words.

text.text: This database provides continuous IRT-based word reading difficulty estimates for 9,961 of the most frequently printed English words for U.S. children in 1 st to 5 th grade, along with detailed wordlevel characteristics, and raw trial-level data.

In what follows, we detail the methods used to collect the data; analytic framework used to establish a continuous measure of word reading difficulty; descriptive statistics of the database; an explanation of the functionality of the publicly available relational database that provides searchable access to word difficulty ratings and associated word-level statistics for each of the stimuli; and finally a demonstration of the d-ELP's ability to estimate the impact of general word-level predictors (e.g., frequency, word length, transparency, semantic measures, and orthographic neighborhood density) on word recognition performance in developing readers.

Data collection procedures varied across the project timeline and are described in three formats (Waves 1-3) for the primary data collection, with supplemental archival data included from a prior study.

Changes to the data collection procedures across Waves 1-3 were made to increase the probability that children would complete their assigned list of words while also trying to maximize the number of responses per word across the sample.

During all aspects of data collection, children worked one-on-one with a trained research assistant in their school, read printed words aloud, and had each response scored as correct or incorrect without performance feedbackfoot_0 .

text.text: For Waves 1-3, children completed only the word reading tasks, with sessions lasting approximately 20 minutes.
In contrast, archival participants completed word reading as part of a larger assessment battery.
Across all data collections, children provided verbal assent at the start of the session, and parental consent was obtained beforehand.
Data collection procedures were approved by the University Institutional Review Board.
Two sets of linking items, comprising 99 total words, were used throughout Waves 1-3; the 63 words from the discontinued WJ3-LWID and 36 words from the NIH Toolbox (LaForte et al., 2024).

Ceiling rules were only used on the WJ3-LWID, as described by the assessment manual, whereas all other items were only scored if the child attempted that item.
For the supplemental archival sample, only the 63 WJ3-LWID words were available as linking items.

The primary purpose of these linking items was to place children and words on a common latent reading scale despite the planned-missing design, in which each child read only a subset of the full item pool.
Because the same linking words were administered across testing forms and cohorts, they served as common anchors that connected otherwise non-overlapping sets of words and participants.

Within the Rasch calibration, performance on the linking items allowed information from individual children to be integrated across forms, enabling the estimation of item difficulties and child reading abilities on a common metric.
In essence, the linking items provided the psychometric bridge needed to support scale identification and comparability across the multiple forms, cohorts, and waves of data collection.
Ceiling rules were applied only to the WJ3-LWID items, following administration procedures described in the assessment manual.
All other words were scored only if attempted by the child.
Children in grades 1-5, 1388 in total, were presented with a list of printed words (paper or tablet) and asked to read those words aloud.
Scores reflected untimed accuracy on each word with words read correctly scored as a 1 and words read incorrectly scored as a 0.
Self-corrections were counted as correct.
The assessment ended immediately if a child became visibly frustrated during the word reading task or asked to stop.
Assessors received training on identifying pronunciations that may have reflected dialectal or speech-related differences rather than incorrect word identification.
When uncertainty arose, assessors documented their observations and audio recordings were reviewed by members of the research team.

Final scoring decisions were informed by both the assessor's notes regarding the child's speech characteristics and the The Developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP) judgment of experienced investigators.

While it is not possible to completely disentangle word recognition difficulties from speech-production factors in an oral reading task, these procedures were implemented to minimize potential scoring errors and ensure consistency in coding. background on an iPad screen.
We had hoped to establish ceiling rules for lists that would allow us to assign all words above the ceiling as attempted and incorrect.
However, there was enough within-and between-child variability on list reading that ceiling rules were deemed impossible, leading us to only score those items that the child attempted.

In Wave 1 we encountered issues of children not finishing their assigned list for various reasons (e.g., inadequate allotment of assessment time or frustration/stamina issues), resulting in some children not attempting all embedded NIH toolbox linking items.
Thus, in The Developmental English Lexicon Project (d-ELP)
Wave 2, all 99 linking items (63 WJ3-LWID and 36 NIH Toolbox) were given first so that all children would attempt all linking items.

Additionally, in Wave 1 the probability that a word would be attempted by a child decreased the further it was on the list (i.e., it was related by how far a child got on the list), and therefore in Wave 2 the order of words was randomized.
Wave 3.
In Wave 3 we worked to better match words difficulty to a child's ability level using initial IRT model results.
This was done by first converting their WJ3-LWID performance to an estimated theta based on a preliminary Rasch model.

Words with the highest standard error (highest standard error items were chosen because it suggested more data is needed for that item) within a range around the estimated theta were selected for reading lists to increase the number of responses.

The range in which words were selected around the estimated theta changed several times during collection of Wave 3 data collection based on feedback from testers to increase the number of responses from children.

The number of pages varied by level with most having 400 words selected but at the lower end fewer words were selected so students would be attempting only the most relevant words, with words randomly ordered and split across lists of 50 words.
Across Waves 1-3 the maximum number of pages to be attempted was 8.

Data from 519 children who attempted 263 of the same words in a prior data collection were added to the d-ELP sample to increase the overall sample size as well as increase the number of attempts for these select words.
These children also completed the WJ3-LWID which served as linking items for this sample.
This sample was presented with words in a traditional paper format.
Children from this data collection have student ids greater than 99000 in the d-ELP database.

Our sampling philosophy for participants was to assess the full range of reading skills across children from the selected grade ranges and allow every child to contribute to the database to the fullest of their ability.

Thus, we did not have strict inclusion/exclusion criteria for participation; however, we did ask teachers to identify children within their classroom for which this study was not appropriate, and these children were excluded from assent and assessment.
All students with parental consent and child assent were eligible to participate.

In rare instances (<0.2% of potential participants), teachers informed the research team that a student was unlikely to be able to meaningfully participate in the assessment due to significant cognitive, behavioral, or communication challenges.

text.text: We trimmed the list of words in the following ways: 1) removed all hyphenated words, words with spaces, and words with apostrophes; 2) removed all first names; 3) retained names of major cities, states, and countries; 4) retained names of historical figures (e.g., Einstein); 5) retained names of groups of people (e.g., Egyptians); 6) removed approximately 1700 simple pluralsaddition of s with no shifts in orthography or phonology (e.g., bats) -to increase the number of unique words in the database; 7) retained plurals that change orthography or phonology (e.g., cities, changes); 8) added back a set of 75 simple plurals (roughly matched to 75 irregular plurals) to allow for a plurals analysis, and 9) removed words that might be considered objectionable to children, teachers, or parents.
This resulted in a list of 10,056 to which we added the linking items.
We applied the difficulty prediction model/routine described above and rank ordered the words from easiest to most difficult.
We selected the first 10,000 words from this list (i.e., eliminating 56 words), retaining all linking items, representing the set of words to sample reading accuracy in children grades 1-5.

Graded word lists were initially constructed for Wave 1 using the rank order list with the NIH linking items mixed throughout the list in position of expected difficulty and the WJ3-LWID removed (these items were administered to identify the grade level list appropriate for each child).
Forty lists were built at each reading grade level (1-5) with the idea that lists would sample from a wide range of difficulties while oversampling at the grade level of the list.

We anticipated that children at a 1 st grade reading level would be able to read fewer words during an assessment session and so 1 st grade lists were 400 words, whereas 2 nd -5 th grade lists contained 500 words.
The Grade Equivalents (GE) of the 63 WJ3-LWID items were used as anchors within the 10,000 words to gauge the general difficulty of words for over sampling at a particular reading grade level.
Sampling for each list varied by reading grade level.

Specifically, 1 st grade lists systematically sampled 200 words rank ordered from 1®1000 difficulty, 100 from the 1001®2000 difficulty, 50 from the 2001 ® 3000 difficulty, and 50 from 3001®5000 difficulty; 2 nd grade lists systematically sampled 100 words from 1®2000 difficulty, 300 from the 2001®5000 difficulty, 50 from the 5001®6000 difficulty, and 50 from 6001®8000 difficulty; 3 nd grade lists systematically sampled 100 words from 1®3000 difficulty, 300 from the 3001®6000 difficulty, 50 from the 6001®7000 difficulty, and 50 from 7001®9000 difficulty; 4 th grade lists systematically sampled 100 words from 1®4000 difficulty, 300 from the 4001®7000 difficulty, 50 from the 7001®8000 difficulty, and 50 from 8001®10000 difficulty; and 5 th grade lists systematically sampled 100 words from 1®4000 difficulty, 100 from the 4001®6000 difficulty, 200 from the 6001®8000 difficulty, and 100 from 8001®10000 difficulty.
Lists within each grade level can be considered roughly equivalent in terms of overall word difficulty with lists becoming systematically more difficult across grade levels.
A majority of the students completed the word reading assessment on an iPad (whereas the first 67 administrations were presented in a typical paper list format).
The iPads were 9th generation iPads with 10.2in retina displays with a resolution of 2160 x 1620 pixels at 264 pixels per inch.
The iPad administration was powered using a Shiny app (Chang et al., 2020) created in R and deployed on the web via shinyapps.io.

text.text: The administration included a two-screen solution such that the child had an iPad and the tester had an iPad each with a unique but linked display.
The tester would first enter the student id into both the student and tester iPad.

This would either bring up the appropriate list for that child (when using preassigned fixed form lists) during Wave 1 or set the seed for word randomization to be the same on both the student and tester versions during Wave 2-3 (for later versions with randomization to ensure words were randomized yet in the same random order on both the student and tester iPads).
The student iPad presented words in black 30-pixel font on a white background arranged in three columns of 25 words each.
Words were presented in lowercase letters except when capitalization was required by standard spelling conventions (e.g., proper nouns).
The "Word" variable in the database reflects the exact word form presented to participants.
The tester iPad looked similar but had a checkbox for scoring next to each word.
Testers would select the words which the child read incorrectly (allowing for unchecking for self-corrections, and data were only sent to the database once the tester hit submit).

In Waves 2 and 3, when a child did not complete the full list, on the page that a child stopped, the tester would click a button that said "stopped on this page" and then select the last item that the child attempted; the rest of the words (which were not attempted) would be entered into the database as missing.
(Wave 1 data underwent a manual data correction procedure to account for where children stopped before this feature was added to the app.)
After completion of a page, both the student and the tester would hit the "Next" button at the bottom right of their screen, which would present the next list to be read.
After the assessment was complete, the tester hit the "submit" button to send the item response data via the web to secure database storage.
Before moving to IRT modeling, items were explored using classical test theory in order to evaluate which items were appropriate to include in the IRT model.
Because of the sampling procedures of items to children, based on expected item difficulty and child ability, proportion correct was not included in this evaluation.
Number of correct and incorrect responses along with item correlations with WJ3-LWID total score were examined.

A total of 67 items were removed from the subsequent IRT analysis for having negative correlations with the latent word difficulty trait or not having at least 2 correct and incorrect responses, suggesting the items estimates were not trustworthy.

These were removed because items with these characteristics may lead to misleading estimates while not necessarily say anything about the item itself given our sampling procedures (i.e., it may just be due to insufficient data for that item).
This resulted in a total of 9,961 items for model fitting and difficulty estimation.
Next, a Rasch model (with planned missing design) was fit to the child-level data using the TAM package (Robitzsch et al., 2024) in R using marginal maximum likelihood estimationfoot_2.

text.text: TAM was selected because it permits estimation of item difficulty in the presence of the planned-missing response structure, in which individual children responded to only a subset of the full item pool.
The final dataset used here consisted of 631,322 total responses from 1907 children across 9,961 words.
This package was selected because it offered the capability to model difficulty in the presence of missing data (i.e., not all children saw all words).
However, it should be noted that these procedures assume that data are missing completely at random.

Although it is true that data were missing because the child did not attempt that word, which words were attempted and not attempted did relate in some way to the child's ability level in at least 2 ways: 1) children were assigned to lists of words to attempt based partially on likely ability level and 2) during Wave 1 words were ordered by potential difficulty with children attempting easier words first, children often ran out of time/energy before completing the list and tended to attempt less words above their ability level.
It's possible that there is some relation between whether an item was attempted and a child's ability level (i.e., difficult words were less likely to be attempted by poor readers).

However, given the linking items attempted by all children span the full range of the item difficulty distribution, we believe this anchored the analysis in a way that allowed for item difficulty to be estimated while taking the ability of the students who attempted that item into account.

Because the number and reading skill of students who attempted each item differed, it's not the case that estimates for items with more attempts are necessarily more precise because the precision of the estimate also depends on whether those students represented an appropriate level of ability for that item.
For this reason, we avoid using number of attempts in the discussion of precision of individual estimates but still present this data in the relational database.
The dataset was collected using a planned-missing design, thus traditional residual-based global fit indices were not computable.

Specifically, the standardized root mean square residuals (SRMR, SRMSR) and Q3-based statistics returned infinite or undefined values, which is expected when item pairs share limited overlap or when some items exhibit near-zero variance among respondents.
Despite this, alternative global fit indices indicated acceptable overall model performance.
The mean absolute deviation of item covariances (100×MADCOV = 3.46) suggested that the Rasch model adequately reproduced the observed covariance structure among items.
The Global Homogeneity Parameter (GHP = 0.33) was lower than the ideal value of 1.0, indicating that the model underestimates the variability present in the observed data.
This underfit likely reflects the sparse response matrix and not substantive model misspecification.

Taken together, the pattern of results suggests that the Rasch model provided a reasonable representation of the data within the constraints of the plannedmissing design, though localized dependencies or multidimensionality cannot be ruled out.

Grade equivalent scores were created by first fitting a function for the WJ3-LWID linking items between the IRT derived difficulty scores and the grade equivalent score from the WJ3-LWID subtest corresponding to the associated raw scores.
Plotting the relation between the IRT derived difficulty and WJ grade equivalent scores revealed a very strong, albeit non-linear, relation (see Figure 3).

text.text: We therefore fitted a function with linear, quadratic, and cubic terms to predict grade equivalence from IRT difficulty, which indeed accounted for 97% of variance in WJ items.
The coefficients from this regression were then used to estimate grade equivalent scores from difficulty scores on the full sample of items.
This variable is referred to as "grade_eq" in the database.

The d-ELP is intended to provide a comprehensive and extensible resource rather than an authoritative source for every lexical characteristic.

Accordingly, the downloadable database preserves the provenance of each variable and enables researchers to substitute or merge alternative lexical variables as appropriate for their research questions.
We anticipate that additional variables and updated lexical measures will be incorporated into future releases of the d-ELP.

text.text: Prior to being granted access to the database, we ask users to register and agree to use the data for noncommercial purposes.
Once access is granted, the interactive database provides multiple tools and pathways for retrieving and exploring the data.
The most basic way is for users to download the full word level database from the Information and Downloads tab.
For users wanting to obtain word characteristics on a specific list of words, the Query tab provides the capability to input words and select which variables to obtain.
Alternatively, the Filter tab can be used to find words that meet certain criteria based on its characteristics, filtering the list based on chosen variables of interest.
Finally, the raw trail data can be directly downloaded via the from the Information and Downloads tab.

The query tab allows users to input (by typing or copying and pasting from excel) a list of words (separated by spaces) for which they would like associated word characteristics, activated through numerous checkboxes, sorted into expandable accordion groups.
Once the user hits submit, the words along with the selected variables will be presented in the table to the right which can be downloaded using the "Download as CSV" button at the top of the table.
Words will appear in rows in the same order that they were entered and any words that do not appear in the database will still appear in the list but will return "NA" for all of the variables.

text.text: The item "abandon" has a difficulty estimate of 1.02 and "abandoned" has 1.07.
While it is reasonable to interpret the difficulty of these words as being close to one another, it is incorrect to conclude that "abandon" is easier than "abandoned".
Looking at the confidence interval, the difficulty of "abandon" is likely to occur anywhere between 0.18 and 1.85 and the difficulty of "abandoned" could be anywhere between 0.08 and 2.06.

With these overlapping ranges, we are unable to say for sure that the true difficulty of "abandon" is easier than "abandoned"; however, it would be appropriate to conclude that both items are easier than "abdomen" which has a difficulty estimate of 4.48 with a plausible value range between 3.32 and 5.63.

And so, while caution is warranted when directly comparing difficulty estimates that are close in value; it is also important to note that the Rasch model empirically orders item difficulties by drawing on the full information available in the data and thus order does matter.

There are numerous potential uses for the d-ELP database.

Here, we present one example illustrating how d-ELP data can be used to evaluate the potential contributions of theoretically important word-level characteristics when included in a model that also contains established word-level characteristics of word difficulty.

In defining a set of established word-level characteristics associated with word reading difficulty, we draw on the work of Strain et al. (2002), who demonstrated the independent contributions of various word characteristics (i.e., including frequency, word length, transparency, semantic variables, and orthographic neighborhood size) to word recognition performance in adult readers.

(2002)</ref>, who demonstrated the independent contributions of various word characteristics (i.e., including frequency, word length, transparency, semantic variables, and orthographic neighborhood size) to word recognition performance in adult readers.

text.text: Our goal here is twofold: (a) to examine whether these word-level characteristics similarly contribute to variation in word difficulty among developing readers and (b) to demonstrate how failure to account for known sources of lexical variance may result in underspecified models that overestimate the importance of less well-established, though theoretically interesting, predictors.

In this set of regression analyses we use the following variables as estimates for established word-level characteristics representing each of the following word traits: frequency (Tasa_sfi), word length (Length), transparency (Spell2pron), semantic measures (Conc_Brys and AoA_Kuper), and neighborhood size (Ortho_N).

We include two sematic measures as a means of highlighting the influence of word semantic characteristics on word reading difficulties in developing readers (see Kellenberger et al., 2024), variables that are often overlooked as control variables in developmental word reading studies.

text.text: The database also includes several alternative frequency measures (e.g., SUBTLEX-US, OpenSubtitles, HAL, and CYP-LEX) to support investigations using different conceptualizations of lexical exposure.
Spell2pron is a consistency rating that asked adults to rate the ease of arriving at a correct pronunciation for a word by applying typical decoding rules.

text.text: Results indicated that words that were longer, less frequent, less transparent, acquired later, and characterized by fewer orthographic neighbors were more difficult to read.
Collectively, these predictors accounted for 64.5% of the variance in word reading difficulty across the 6,397 words.

We note, that although orthographic neighbors may increase lexical competition in some recognition tasks, larger orthographic neighborhoods have frequently been associated with facilitative effects in word naming, particularly among developing readers, presumably because they provide greater support from familiar orthographic patterns (for details see, Andrews, 1997; Carreiras, Perea, & Grainger, 1997).

text.text: In these models the unique R² associated with each of the variables (represented by DR²) was estimated by block entering the other five variables followed by adding the variable of interest.

Overall, DR² values ranged from .02% to 11.2% of the variance, with the magnitude of unique contributions rank ordered (from largest to smallest) as follows: age of acquisition, transparency, orthographic neighborhood size, frequency, length, and concreteness.

While the results clearly suggest there is considerable shared variance among the 6 predictors (67.9% of the explained variance is shared) there is a sizeable amount of the variance that is unique to the various predictors (32.1% of the variance explained is unique).

Notably, variables representing age of acquisition, transparency, and orthographic neighborhood size accounted for the largest portion of unique variance but are largely missing as word-level predictors in developmental experiential and individual differences studies of word reading.

This is one example of how the d-ELP can allow researchers to improve their work by providing an evidence-based way to decide which variables to include (here as control variables, but possibly as independent variable as well) in their experimental designs.

The English orthography is best described as quasiregular, consisting of a complex interplay between morphological regularities, syllabic constraints, and numerous sub-lexical regularities in spelling-sound correspondences.

For this reason, English presents a set of unique and significant challenges for children as they work to develop efficient and automatic word reading skills (see Seymour, 2013; Seymour et al., 2003), with individual differences in word reading development representing a complex interaction between the property of words and the skills and knowledge that children bring to the process of learning to read (e.g., Steacy et al., 2022).

text.text: Teasing out these complex interactions has been difficult due to the complex task of characterizing "word difficulty" from a developmental word reading perspective.

The inability to precisely quantify word difficulty empirically across the wide range of words encountered during reading development has also been related to the lack of a large-scale developmental word reading database.
To help alleviate these issues we developed the d-ELP database of word reading performance in a diverse sample of US children.

In this first paper, we use these data to derive IRT-based estimates of oral word-reading difficulty on a common developmental scale across a broad range of words and to identify several key word-level characteristics that should be considered in future studies of word reading.
As with previous "lexicon projects" we have made our representational database publicly accessible, along with downloadable raw trail data, through the use of an interactive Shiny app.

We believe this initial iteration of the d-ELP, and any subsequent versions, will have important educational, psychological, and computational uses going forward that will improve our basic understanding of reading development and practices of improving reading outcomes for children.

Placing the 9,961 most frequently printed English words on a continuous difficulty scale represents a major advancement in promoting the understanding and modeling of word reading difficulty across the early reading developmental span.
However, this achievement is best viewed as a foundational step.

Because it is impractical to ask children to attempt all 9,961 words, the resulting database necessarily has limitations for modeling child-by-word interactions across both a wide developmental range and a large corpus of words (for details, see Keuleers, Diependaele, & Brysbaert, 2010).

text.text: In addition, the word characteristics contained in the d-ELP were "harvested" from other open-source databases (e.g., CELEX; Baayen, Piepenbrock, & Gulikers, 1993; ELP; Balota et al., 2007; SCOPE; Gao et al., 2023) without any type of verification other than spot checks that the merging processes at the level of the item were accurate.

text.text: This introduces two immediate problems: 1) there are inaccuracies/inconsistencies in some of the specific word characteristics variables within these mega-database (e.g., number of morphemes and syllables, stress pattern designation, and age-of-acquisition measures) further complicated by discrepancies occurring across sources and 2) many of the existing word variables we include in the d-ELP are based on adult corpus (e.g., orthographic-semantic consistency, frequency, semantic diversity, etc.) or adult ratings (e.g., spelling-to-pronunciation transparency, familiarity, concreteness, etc.).

As such, these word characteristics may not necessary be appropriate as measures representing word characteristics in children by systematically overestimating the strengths of word representations as predictors (see Kuperman & Van Dyke, 2013 for the case of age-of-acquisition).
text.formatted: As such, these word characteristics may not necessary be appropriate as measures representing word characteristics in children by systematically overestimating the strengths of word representations as predictors (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Kuperman & Van Dyke, 2013</ref> for the case of age-of-acquisition).

text.text: In terms of addressing the first issue, we recommend that when using the d-ELP some verification be done on variables known to be subjective in nature or containing inaccuracies.

For the second issue we suggest whenever possible using word variables based on child corpus or child rating; keeping in mind there are often not parallel word characteristic variables based on children and adults.

Going forward we acknowledge the need to compute and validate "child-directed measures" for many word characteristic measures used in developmental reading studies; we believe that the d-ELP data would be useful in validating such new quantifications.
And finally, subgroup comparisons by ethnicity or language ability were outside the scope of the present study and were not conducted.

Nonetheless, the d-ELP provides a powerful tool for selecting words that match specific developmental periods and linguistic characteristics, thereby facilitating more precise and targeted data collection in which children can reasonably attempt all items.
We emphasize that this initial iteration of the d-ELP represents a first step toward a more comprehensive understanding of how word characteristics influence reading difficulty in developing readers.

The precision of the current word difficulty estimates is constrained by the number of child-level observations per item, but we aim to establish a mechanism for researchers to contribute additional data to improve item calibration, similar to our integration of archival data in the present study.
In this sense, the d-ELP serves as an initial, open-ended framework for estimating and refining word reading difficulty across development.
